desc:
Coins of the distinct values in coins are available in unlimited quantity. Count the combinations that add up to exactly amount and use at most k coins in total. The order of the coins does not matter: 1+2 and 2+1 are the same combination.

Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007. The empty combination counts as one way to make amount = 0.

coins = [1,2,5], amount = 5, k = 2 -> 1   (5)
coins = [1,2,5], amount = 5, k = 3 -> 2   (5 and 1+2+2)
coins = [1,2,5], amount = 5, k = 5 -> 4   (5, 1+2+2, 1+1+1+2, 1+1+1+1+1)
constraints: 1 ≤ coins[i] ≤ 1,000 and all values are distinct
hints: The unordered coin-change count uses one dimension (the sum). Here the number of coins used matters too, so you need a second dimension.

Let ways[j][s] be the number of combinations of exactly j coins that sum to s, using the coin values handled so far. Handle one value c at a time, in the outer loop, to keep the combinations unordered.
For each coin c, for j = 1..k ascending and s = c..amount ascending: ways[j][s] += ways[j - 1][s - c]. The answer is the sum of ways[j][amount] over j = 0..k.
editorial: Counting unordered combinations requires the outer loop to run over coin values, with the inner loops extending the combinations by that value; this way each multiset is built in exactly one order (all coins of the first value, then of the next, and so on). To enforce the limit on the number of coins, extend the state by the coin count: ways[j][s] is the number of combinations of exactly j coins with total s.

Adding any number of copies of coin c is the usual unbounded update ways[j][s] += ways[j - 1][s - c]. For this to be correct, iterate j upward, so that ways[j - 1][s - c] already contains combinations that use c (which allows several copies of c). Finally add up ways[j][amount] for j from 0 to k. Time is O(n · k · amount), space O(k · amount).
